egypt_evidence_status.interpretation: The Egypt-only search did not locate a reliable Egyptian field survey, isolate record, or official distribution entry confirming Kabatiella zeae eyespot on maize in Egypt.
egypt_evidence_status.important_negative_evidence: A 2022 Egyptian survey of seed-borne and toxigenic fungi examined maize samples from 25 governorates, but the reported frequent fungi did not include K. zeae. This does not prove absence from Egypt because the survey focused on seed/grain-associated fungi rather than a dedicated foliar-disease survey.
egypt_evidence_status.global_context: Eyespot is associated mainly with cool, moist maize-growing environments and is reported in parts of Asia, Europe, North America, and South America.

early_stage: Small, light-coloured or translucent circular spots
Spots may look water-soaked when young
A narrow yellow chlorotic halo surrounds the spot
characteristic_eyespot: Round to oval lesions, approximately 1–4 mm in diameter
Distinct red-brown, dark-brown, purple, or black ring around the centre
The centre-and-ring pattern creates a visible eye-like appearance
Lesions may be most numerous along leaf margins and near veins
advanced_stage: Lesions darken and may become necrotic
The lesion centre can fall out, leaving a shot-hole appearance
Many lesions may merge into larger dead areas
Leaves yellow and die at infection sites
Leaf sheaths and husks covering ears may also develop spots and shrivel
image_annotation_targets: lesion position near veins or leaf margins

lesion_dimensions.egypt_specific_measurement: Not available because an Egypt-specific field record was not confirmed.

distribution_on_plant: In documented disease descriptions, lesions occur mainly on older leaves, often along leaf margins and veins; leaf sheaths and ear-covering leaves can also be affected. Egypt-specific canopy distribution is unconfirmed.
progression: Small translucent or light-coloured spots appear, often with a yellow halo.
Spots develop tan centres and dark red-brown, purple, or black rings.
The characteristic eye-like lesions multiply, especially under cool, wet conditions.
Lesions darken, coalesce, and form necrotic areas; centres may fall out.
Leaves yellow, dry, and die at the infection sites, potentially reducing grain filling when infection is early and severe.

environment.humidity: High humidity, frequent dew, rain, and extended leaf wetness favour infection and conidial production.
environment.temperature: Cool conditions are most favourable; approximately 10–12 °C is reported as highly favourable for maize susceptibility in disease references.
environment.residue: Infected maize residue is the main reported source of primary inoculum; continuous maize and reduced/no-tillage systems can increase risk.
environment.egypt_context: Cool, wet conditions are less typical of much of Egypt's maize-growing season than the environments where eyespot is normally important. This is a risk interpretation and not evidence that the disease is absent or present in Egypt.

similar_diseases.name: Gray Leaf Spot
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Produces longer, rectangular grey-to-tan lesions restricted by leaf veins rather than small ringed eye-like spots.

similar_diseases.name: Common Rust
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Produces raised powdery orange-brown pustules, not flat tan-centred lesions with dark rings.

similar_diseases.name: Insect feeding or aphid injury
similar_diseases.visual_difference: May create small spots or shot holes but normally lacks the consistent tan-centre, dark-ring, yellow-halo pattern.

similar_diseases.name: Nutrient deficiency or herbicide injury
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Can cause chlorosis or spotting but does not normally form discrete eye-like lesions with a defined dark ring.

recommended_image_search_terms: suspected maize eyespot Egypt Kabatiella zeae
maize eyespot tan centre purple ring yellow halo
diagnostic_caution: Because Egypt-specific confirmation was not located, an Egyptian sample with eye-like spots should be treated as suspected eyespot only. Confirm with fungal isolation and microscopic identification of Kabatiella conidia/conidiomata or molecular testing.
